newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi sanctions fail in political aim, report.
newsitem.headline: Burundi sanctions fail in political aim, report.

text.p: A study of sanctions imposed on Burundi by regional states found no hard evidence they had succeeded in their political aims while smuggling was weakening their impact.
The findings were overall a blow to proponents of sanctions, with Burundi as the latest international case of states using embargoes in a bid to force stubborn foreign rulers to buckle.

Initial findings issued on Tuesday by the U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA) suggested Burundi sanctions should be re-targeted to protect the vulnerable and more items exempted for aid agencies.

"While it is possible that concessions by the regime may, in part, be the result of prolonged sanctions, there is no concrete evidence that sanctions have been (politically) successful," said researchers from Brown University in the United States.
"Although the willingness of the Burundi regime to undertake unconditional negotiations is an important and positive step, whether it resulted from pressure due to sanctions is unknown."

The preliminary report was released by DHA in Nairobi on the eve of a summit of regional leaders in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha to review sanctions since July 31 last year to force military ruler Pierre Buyoya into talks with Hutu rebels.

"A combination of profiteering, insecurity, lack of enforcement and weakening political resolve has resulted in a high level of smuggling and cross-border trade which have diluted sanctions' impact," the report for DHA said.
The report noted that smuggling and humanitarian aid had become the only two sources of imported essential goods.

"Sanctions have therefore created shortages of fuel, raw materials, retail goods, spare parts, agricultural inputs and medicine. Those items still available (through smuggling) are available at high cost to the consumer.

"The result has been hyper-inflation, paralysis of the commercial and industrial sectors of the economy, loss of income and rising unemployment," said the report, adding Bujumbura port on Lake Tanganyika had closed as had factories in the capital.
The report said sanctions hit the five percent of Burundi's population in urban areas harder than subsistence farmers in rural areas, who were still short of seeds and fertilisers.
In particular, the report said sanctions were hard on aid agencies as exemptions were slowly granted for some items and higher costs forced agencies to reduce the scope of programmes.
Aid agencies had even had to buy fuel on the black market at high cost until exemptions for fuel were approved, it said.
It added sanctions-breaking air corridors had been set up between Bujumbura and African and European countries and fuel and other basic supplies were imported and coffee was exported.
"A high rate of smuggling exists across borders with neighbouring countries. The border with eastern Zaire is porous, facilitating unhindered movement of goods," the report said.

"Sanctions have, in many ways, increased tensions between the Burundi regime and neighbouring countries," said the report, adding the military-appointed government had some success in portraying sanctions as an attack on people rather than itself.

The seizure of east Zaire since October by Tutsi-dominated rebels has benefitted Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army because Hutu rebels based in Zaire were uprooted. Kinshasa has accused Burundi of sending its troops into Zaire to aid the rebellion.

Burundi's government denies such accusations, as does Rwanda and Uganda. Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Zaire and Zambia said when they imposed sanctions that they expected them to achieve their main objectives within one to two months.
